title: What If It Never Rained Again? The Sky Holds Ten Days of Water

scenes.text: What if it never rained again? The first surprise: the sky barely holds any water.
All the water vapour in the atmosphere, dropped at once, would cover the planet about 2.5 centimetres deep. One inch.
A water molecule spends only about ten days in the air before it falls. Rain is the planet recycling almost half a million cubic kilometres a year.
Rivers hold roughly 1,200 cubic kilometres in total. Within weeks of the last storm, most of them are shrinking.
Without rain, the oceans keep evaporating, so the air gets wetter and heavier but never lets go. Lakes drop, soil hardens, crops fail across whole continents.
Earth would still have 97 percent of its water. It would just all be in the sea, and none of it would be coming back to you.

description:
What if it never rained again? The atmosphere holds only about 12,900 cubic kilometres of water, enough to cover Earth about 2.5 centimetres deep if it all fell at once, and a water molecule stays airborne only around ten days before it precipitates. Roughly half a million cubic kilometres evaporate from land and sea every year and come back as rain and snow.
With that cycle broken, the roughly 1,200 cubic kilometres held in all the world's rivers would shrink within weeks, lakes and soils would dry, and the oceans would keep the water that never returns.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: About 90 percent of the water in the air came from oceans and lakes, and 10 percent from plants breathing it out. What should never happen again? Drop your own what-if below.
